rv.q: Water for Elephants isn't just the frontrunner for the 2024. Tony Award for Best Musical, it's a bold assertion that this still young artform has plenty of tricks left to reveal.
"Water for Elephants” could be the greatest show on Broadway.

In building such a huge and heart-filling musical one image at a time, the creators of “Water for Elephants” have disproved the old circus adage behind the title, which holds that you can never deliver enough sustenance for a creature so large and thirsty.
The result is one of the most authentic circus-themed shows to make it to Broadway.
At first, Rosie simply appears as a pair of legs.
The main attraction is the pull of the circus itself.
Not everything works in Jessica Stone’s production — there’s a reason the words “dream sequence” tend to set off alarm bells — but at least it summons a coherent theatrical universe.

Clear away the schmaltz, and there are bodies in space stretching and twisting toward something strange and sublime, bodies that pulse with e. e. cummings’s fervent cry: “Damn everything but the circus!”

Still, the largely pasteurized manner in which the musical depicts the often-sordid lives of circus folk of the period lends “Water for Elephants” an anodyne weightlessness, at least until the denouement.
Thankfully, it’s rescued from total banality by a group of wonderful acrobats, who double as carnies and animals, and have an irrepressible desire to entertain.
The circus and the theatre may have a lot in common, but there's little of the thrill of either here.
Water for Elephants grabs that magic and makes it fly.
Here, she amplifies her florid material without blowing it out of proportion, giving us a continuously engaging evening without overselling its significance.
By any measure, Water for Elephants is a spectacular display of theatrical collaboration at its best, and it should have wide appeal to kinkers and rubes alike.
The musical version of Water for Elephants is one of the few film-to-stage adaptations in many years to be as successful as the cinema version.
With its key infusion of circus artistry, this production of Water for Elephants is a delightful musical diversion.
Unlike some other literary adaptations in the works or already on the boards, this production stands on its own merits as theatre.

Water for Elephants is a sweeping spectacle that manages to capture both the grandeur and intimacy of Sara Gruen's beloved novel. The production succeeds in creating theatrical magic through stunning puppetry and heartfelt performances.

Much else in “Water for Elephants” has its pleasures – the score, the singing, the puppetry, the acting, even the love story — but nothing else matches the circus artistry for its originality, variety and consistency.
The romance may fall short, and the songs lack a certain luster, but the magic of the circus is winning.
Unfortunately, it’s also far from being the greatest show on Earth.

It’s now turning dazzling somersaults—both on stage and in playgoers’ hearts—at the Imperial Theatre in a captivating production with a delightful score by the seven-member collective called the PigPen Theatre Co.
But Water for Elephants feels more clunky than transporting.
Because Gustin and McCalla are stuck playing such colorless characters, it leaves Nolan’s wild and demented August to carry the show.
But the magic is fleeting, and by the final curtain, those in the audience may wish they'd just stayed at home.
Water for Elephants is a must-see and shows us how Grant Gustin should have been on Broadway all along.
It was stunning to see the exquisite work, to hold your breath as the kinkers performed their magic moves.

The themes of love, fortitude, old age, grief, cold-heartedness, hope, and redemption are woven throughout every scene making “Water for Elephants” one of the most heartwarming productions on Broadway this season.
Although “Water for Elephants” is a musical about a circus, I wouldn't bring our 11- year old.
“Water for Elephants” wins on choreography, puppetry and acrobatic wonder.
Water for Elephants is a thoroughly dazzling theatre experience.
Regardless, it is quite a spectacle and still worth more than just a passing glance, especially since it is feel-good escapism.

cn.t: Critics praise the remarkable circus ensemble and stunning acrobatics, but find the Depression-era love story formulaic and the score forgettable, making for a visually dazzling spectacle that lacks emotional depth.

vs.sum: The Imperial Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and solid sound quality, though some seats may miss minor stage action. While the ambiance is enhanced by its historic architectural design, comfort is average with decent legroom. Facilities are lacking, with long restroom lines being a common issue.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair locations in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.

vr.q: If you are somebody that loves spectacle and wants to see wow moments on a stage, this is your show for sure.
